## Introduction
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is an autonomic nervous system disorder characterized by an excessive heart rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute (or 40 beats per minute in adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, often accompanied by symptoms such as lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations.1,2 Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a group of connective tissue disorders that result in hypermobile joints, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.3 Both conditions are increasingly recognized to occur concurrently with mast cell activation disorders (MCADs), which represent a spectrum of conditions involving inappropriate mast cell activation and mediator release. MCADs include mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS; most frequently associated condition), idiopathic, monoclonal, and secondary types, including systemic mastocytosis.4 Another condition, hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), has been associated with more severe symptoms in patients with IgE and non–IgE-mediated mast cell activation, especially in patients with venom allergy, and possibly in mastocytosis.5
Although anecdotal and clinical observations suggest a potential relationship among POTS, EDS, and MCADs/HAT, the evidence supporting this association remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MCADs and HAT in patients diagnosed with having EDS and/or POTS.

# The relationship between mast cell activation syndrome, postural tachycardia syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
## Cite this
N2 - Background: Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) can occur in the same patient. In this study, we investigated the relationship among these three syndromes. Objective: To establish the relationship of MCAS in patients diagnosed with POTS and hypermobile EDS as well as characterize the demographics of the patients affected by these syndromes. Methods: A total of 195 medical records of patients by using a diagnostic codes data base search for disorders of autonomic dysfunction were identified. The demographics of the patients and diagnoses of POTS, EDS, or MCAS were recorded. Confidence intervals of the proportion of patients MCAS within a population of patients with POTS and EDS were compared with the proportion of patients with MCAS and without POTS and EDS. Odds ratios were also calculated within these groups. Results: The percentage of MCAS within the group of POTS and EDS was 31% in comparison with 2% within the non-POTS and EDS group. The 95% confidence interval calculated for the MCAS in the POTS and EDS group did not overlap with 2%, which showed a statistically significant result. The odds ratio between the two groups was found to be 32.46. Conclusion: There was a marked percentage of MCAS among the patients with diagnoses of POTS and EDS.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
Why joint pain, digestion, histamine reactions, and energy all trace back to the same physiology.
A person with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome may walk into one appointment for joint pain, another for digestive problems, another for dizziness, and another for unexplained reactions to foods, supplements, medications, heat, exercise, or hormonal changes.
Each symptom can look like it belongs to a different body system. Connective tissue links these systems together.
Connective tissue provides structure, elasticity, mechanical stability, and support throughout the body. It surrounds joints, blood vessels, nerves, muscles, organs, the digestive tract, and immune cells. When connective tissue is lax, fragile, or mechanically unstable, the effects extend far beyond flexibility.
This broader physiology explains why people with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, hypermobile EDS, or hypermobility spectrum disorder often experience pain, fatigue, digestive dysfunction, autonomic instability, migraines, allergies, histamine symptoms, sleep disruption, and nervous-system sensitivity together.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## What Are Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders?
The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are a group of inherited connective-tissue conditions. The 2017 international classification recognizes 13 EDS subtypes. Most have known disease-associated genes and can be investigated through clinical genetic testing.
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, commonly called hEDS, remains the main exception. A single validated causative gene has not yet been established for most affected people, so diagnosis remains clinical.
**Common features of hEDS include:**
*   Generalized joint hypermobility and instability  
*   Musculoskeletal pain, subluxations, and dislocations  
*   Soft or mildly hyperextensible skin and easy bruising  
*   Pelvic-floor problems, hernias, and dental crowding  
*   Fatigue, digestive symptoms, and autonomic symptoms
Hypermobility spectrum disorder, or HSD, describes symptomatic joint hypermobility that causes pain, instability, injury, or fatigue without meeting the full criteria for hEDS or another connective-tissue disorder.
Some people are visibly flexible. Others lose flexibility with age, injury, pain, muscular guarding, or arthritis. A person may have performed splits or repeatedly sprained joints as a child, yet appear stiff in adulthood. One examination does not fully describe a lifetime of connective-tissue behavior.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## The Symptom Pattern We See Most Often
Among clients identified with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or clinically significant hypermobility, these symptoms appeared most frequently.
52%Anxiety or panic
46%Gastrointestinal dysfunction
44%Mast-cell or histamine symptoms
42%Chronic fatigue or ME/CFS
42%Chronic or widespread pain
38%Significant sleep problems
38%Allergies or sensitivities
34%POTS or dysautonomia
28%ADHD, autism, neurodivergence
24%Migraines or frequent headaches
Additional connective-tissue features included joint instability, subluxations, easy bruising, pelvic-floor dysfunction, prolapse, poor wound healing, labral injuries, tendon problems, and recurrent musculoskeletal injuries.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## Bringing the Whole Pattern Together
Joint instability can increase muscle guarding. Muscle guarding can increase pain and energy demand. Poor sleep can increase pain sensitivity and mast-cell reactivity. Dysautonomia can increase adrenaline, dizziness, and fatigue. Gastrointestinal dysfunction can reduce nutrient absorption. Histamine can affect sleep, heart rate, digestion, and nervous-system activation. Genetic variants shape how efficiently each pathway responds.
This interconnected physiology is why supporting one symptom in isolation often produces limited results. Someone with POTS, low ferritin, DAO-related histamine pressure, and slower COMT needs a different plan from someone whose primary concern is tendon injury with otherwise stable digestion and circulation. Gene variants are indicators of nutritional load and physiological tendency, not diagnoses or fixed outcomes.
Your symptoms carry information about circulation, nervous-system activity, connective-tissue demand, digestion, immune signaling, and nutrient handling. Genetics can add another layer of clarity. Laboratory testing can identify correctable deficiencies. Careful tracking can reveal triggers. A physiology-first, genetics-informed approach brings these systems together and allows nutrients to be selected with intention, at a pace your body can actually use.

# The relationship between mast cell activation syndrome, postural tachycardia syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
## Cite this
N2 - Background: Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) can occur in the same patient. In this study, we investigated the relationship among these three syndromes. Objective: To establish the relationship of MCAS in patients diagnosed with POTS and hypermobile EDS as well as characterize the demographics of the patients affected by these syndromes. Methods: A total of 195 medical records of patients by using a diagnostic codes data base search for disorders of autonomic dysfunction were identified. The demographics of the patients and diagnoses of POTS, EDS, or MCAS were recorded. Confidence intervals of the proportion of patients MCAS within a population of patients with POTS and EDS were compared with the proportion of patients with MCAS and without POTS and EDS. Odds ratios were also calculated within these groups. Results: The percentage of MCAS within the group of POTS and EDS was 31% in comparison with 2% within the non-POTS and EDS group. The 95% confidence interval calculated for the MCAS in the POTS and EDS group did not overlap with 2%, which showed a statistically significant result. The odds ratio between the two groups was found to be 32.46. Conclusion: There was a marked percentage of MCAS among the patients with diagnoses of POTS and EDS.

Title: The Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome Connection
Chunks: 0,1,3,4
**By Dr. David Traster, DC, MS, DACNB**
Co-owner, _The Neurologic Wellness Institute_
Boca Raton • Chicago • Waukesha • Wood Dale www.neurologicwellnessinstitute.com
For many years, patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) were often told that their symptoms existed in isolation. Joint pain was considered orthopedic. Dizziness was considered autonomic. Rashes and flushing were considered allergic. Gastrointestinal symptoms were considered functional. Fatigue was blamed on stress. Yet over time, clinicians began noticing a pattern that was difficult to ignore: many patients with hypermobility also demonstrated symptoms consistent with abnormal mast cell activity.
Today, there is growing interest in the overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). While the relationship is still being actively studied, clinical observations and emerging research suggest these conditions frequently coexist and may influence one another in meaningful ways.
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by joint hypermobility, tissue fragility, chronic pain, and widespread multisystem involvement. Unlike some other forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the exact genetic cause of hEDS remains unclear in most cases.
Connective tissue is everywhere in the body. It supports joints, stabilizes blood vessels, forms fascia, lines the gastrointestinal tract, and plays a role in nervous system structure and signaling. When connective tissue is altered, as it is in hEDS, the effects can extend far beyond the musculoskeletal system.
Many individuals with hEDS experience:
*   Joint instability and pain

*   Chronic fatigue

*   Brain fog

*   Dizziness or POTS-like symptoms

*   Gastrointestinal dysfunction

*   Headaches

*   Flushing and skin sensitivity

*   Medication intolerance

*   Allergic-type symptoms
This broad symptom profile is one reason mast cell involvement has become an area of interest.
Mast cells are immune cells that reside primarily within connective tissue. They act as frontline responders, especially in areas exposed to the external environment such as the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

When activated, mast cells release chemical mediators including histamine, tryptase, cytokines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. These substances help coordinate immune responses and inflammation. In normal physiology, this is protective. But when mast cells become dysregulated, they may release these mediators excessively or inappropriately.
In Mast Cell Activation Syndrome, this dysregulation can lead to symptoms such as:
*   Flushing

*   Itching or hives

*   Gastrointestinal distress

*   Rapid heart rate

*   Dizziness

*   Brain fog

*   Fatigue

*   Headaches

*   Sensitivity to foods, chemicals, or medications

*   Blood pressure instability
Because mast cells live inside connective tissue, researchers began questioning whether abnormalities in connective tissue could influence mast cell behavior.
One of the most consistent observations in clinical practice is that individuals with hEDS appear to have higher rates of mast-cell-related symptoms. This has led to several proposed mechanisms explaining the overlap.
Mast cells are embedded in connective tissue. In hEDS, the extracellular matrix and collagen structure are altered. This means mast cells are functioning within a different physical and biochemical environment than normal.
Some researchers propose that these structural changes may lower the activation threshold of mast cells or make them more reactive to mechanical stress. Everyday forces such as stretch, pressure, or micro-injury could potentially trigger exaggerated mast cell responses. This concept falls under mechanobiology, where physical properties of tissue influence cellular behavior.
The relationship may also be bidirectional. Mast cells release substances like histamine and proteases that can influence connective tissue integrity, vascular permeability, and inflammatory signaling.
Over time, this may contribute to:
*   Increased tissue laxity

*   Vascular instability

*   Chronic inflammation

*   Impaired tissue repair
This creates a potential feedback loop:
abnormal connective tissue influences mast cells, and activated mast cells further impact connective tissue.
Another major point of overlap is dysautonomia.
Many individuals with hEDS experience symptoms such as:
*   Orthostatic intolerance

*   POTS

*   Heart rate variability

*   Blood pressure instability

*   Heat intolerance

*   Gastrointestinal dysmotility

The overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome represents a complex and evolving area of medicine. While definitive answers are still emerging, the clinical patterns are difficult to ignore.
For many patients, this connection helps make sense of a constellation of symptoms that once seemed unrelated. It suggests that the body’s structural framework, immune system, and nervous system are not operating independently, but as part of a highly interconnected network.
As research continues to evolve, this relationship may offer important insights into not only hEDS and MCAS, but the broader understanding of chronic multisystem conditions and the biology that connects them.

## What are dysautonomia and POTS?
The autonomic nervous system regulates body functions that normally occur without conscious effort, including heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, sweating, temperature control, pupil responses, bladder function, and digestion.
The sympathetic nervous system helps the body respond to exertion or stress. The parasympathetic nervous system supports recovery, digestion, energy conservation, and the slowing of heart rate after a demand has passed. Dysautonomia occurs when one or more aspects of this automatic regulation do not function normally.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, is one form of orthostatic intolerance. Current diagnostic criteria generally require chronic orthostatic symptoms together with a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute in adults—or 40 beats per minute in adolescents—within 10 minutes of standing or head-up tilt, without the blood-pressure fall required to diagnose orthostatic hypotension. Other causes of tachycardia must also be excluded. **(1)**(opens in new tab)
POTS can involve different and overlapping mechanisms, including low circulating blood volume, excessive venous pooling, partial autonomic neuropathy, high sympathetic activation, deconditioning, immune-related factors, and secondary medical conditions. The diagnosis therefore describes a physiological pattern; it does not by itself identify the cause.
Common symptoms include:
*   Lightheadedness, blurred vision, weakness, or near-fainting while upright  
*   Palpitations and a rapid heart rate after standing  
*   Exercise intolerance and prolonged fatigue  
*   Headache, brain fog, and impaired concentration  
*   Nausea, abdominal discomfort, bloating, constipation, or diarrhea  
*   Heat intolerance and abnormal sweating  
*   Tremulousness, sleep disturbance, and sensations that may resemble anxiety
